claims.text: The initial protective coating is a nanostructured, multiphase high-entropy alloy containing FCC and BCC phases with coherent interphase boundaries.
Coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries create local misfit stress fields.
The local stress fields associated with coherent phase boundaries pin dislocations.
Coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries retard diffusion-driven dislocation climb.
Dislocation pinning and retarded climb enhance the coating's creep resistance under continuous loading.
Processing a similarly composed alloy to favor a predominantly FCC single phase can produce a comparison material lacking significant coherent phase boundaries.
The high-entropy alloy exhibits inherently sluggish elemental diffusion.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces slow dislocation glide.
Sluggish diffusion and coherent-interface pinning slow dislocation climb.
Slower dislocation glide and climb impede time-dependent plastic deformation.
Under identical sustained loading and temperature, the mixed FCC/BCC coating will have a lower creep strain rate than the predominantly single-phase FCC baseline.
At sufficiently high temperatures, rapid diffusion may diminish the creep-resistance benefit associated with coherent phase boundaries.
At stresses exceeding the dislocation-pinning capacity of the microstructure, the creep-resistance benefit may diminish.
Grain size may influence the measured creep behavior.
Minor compositional variations may influence the measured creep behavior.
